name: head
one_line: output the first part of files
plain: `head` prints the beginning of a file: by default the first 10 lines. It lets you peek at a big file without opening all of it.
In security work it is the quickest look at a log, a CSV, a wordlist or the first bytes of a binary.
when: See what a big log or data file looks like.
Keep only the top results of a ranked list (sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head).
Cut a file to its first N bytes, for example to test a header.

examples.title: First 10 lines
examples.explain: With no option you get the first ten lines. Handy to learn the layout of a log before you search it.

examples.title: A chosen number of lines  (-n)
examples.explain: Prints the first three lines. head -3 is a short way to write the same thing.

examples.title: All but the last 2 lines  (-n -2)
examples.explain: A negative number means 'everything except the last N lines'. Useful for dropping a footer.

examples.title: The first bytes of a file  (-c)
examples.explain: -c counts bytes, not lines. Together with xxd you see the magic number of a file without reading all of it.

examples.title: Top of a ranked list
examples.cmd: awk '{print $1}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -3
examples.explain: The classic counting pipeline ends with head to keep only the three busiest IPs.

examples.title: Several files at once
examples.explain: When you give several files head prints a header line with each file's name. -q hides the headers and -v forces them even for one file.

options.plain: Print the first NUM bytes. With a minus sign, print everything except the last NUM bytes.
options.use: Reading a file header or trimming bytes.

options.plain: Print the first NUM lines (default 10). With a minus sign, everything except the last NUM lines.
Never print the file-name headers when you give several files.
options.use: You want one clean stream of text.

options.plain: Always print the file-name header, even for a single file.
Treat NUL bytes, not newlines, as the end of a line.
Print a short usage message and exit.

mistakes: head -n 1 file only reads the start; it does not tell you the file has more lines.
On a binary file the output can garble your terminal: use head -c N file | xxd instead.
A size suffix works (head -c 1K) but means 1024 bytes, while 1KB means 1000.
try: Show the first line of every .txt file in a folder, with names.
Print the header row of a CSV.
Cut a file in half by line count with wc -l and head.
see_also: tail(1), less(1), cat(1), sed(1) (sed -n '1,5p'), awk(1), xxd(1).
captured_with: Examples are written to explain a technique; they are not captured output.
